rationale: A wins because it finds the live reporting door, not just the launch wrapper: “Anker is betting homeowners skip home batteries because of the installation job, not the price” is arguable, testable, and paired with the electrician proof it needs. B is competent, but “The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery” and “Why a phone-charger giant is betting on home energy storage” are two jackets on the same brand-extension story. A also does the harder PR work: it refuses the tempting bill-savings, IRA, customer, and data angles instead of quietly wishing them into existence.
gaps_in_A: “Anker just set the timeline” overclaims. One US launch is a signal, not a market timetable, unless backed by the comparable-company pattern A says it still needs.
“The installation barrier has been cited repeatedly as the main friction point” is not in the supplied facts. Source it or recast it as the question a reporter should test.
“not the price” is too neat. The update gives a no-rewiring claim, not consumer research showing installation beats price as the adoption blocker.
gaps_in_B: “The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery” and “Why a phone-charger giant is betting on home energy storage” are too close. Brand trust and corporate strategy are separable, but here they still smell like the same sandwich.
It buries the best concrete product claim. “installs without major electrical rewiring” belongs as its own homeowner/adoption angle, not just proof language under the Tesla comparison.
“Anker naming Tesla Powerwall as direct competition” overstates the record. The update says Anker competes with Powerwall; it does not say Anker named Tesla.
“deploying capital into an unfamiliar, competitive category” is a plausible inference, but B has no spend, R&D, revenue target, or investor signal. The proof list admits the angle is underfed.
